[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of recent minimum wage increases in U.S. cities (e.g., Seattle, San Francisco, Los Angeles) using difference-in-differences or synthetic control methods, focusing on low-skilled workers' formal vs. informal employment transitions via administrative payroll data and household surveys. — Directly tests the hypothesis in the specified geographic and temporal scope, providing causal estimates of the effect on informal sector participation and formal employment within 12 months.

[PATH:empirical] Survey-based longitudinal panel data on informal sector participation among low-skilled workers in high-cost urban areas, such as the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY) or Current Population Survey (CPS) matched with state/city minimum wage records, analyzed with fixed-effects models. — Allows measurement of individual-level transitions between formal and informal work following minimum wage changes, controlling for unobserved heterogeneity and local labor market conditions.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of dual labor markets with endogenous informal sector size, such as search-and-matching models incorporating minimum wage and enforcement, calibrated to U.S. urban settings. — Provides a formal framework to predict the conditions under which the hypothesized mechanism (increased opportunity cost of informal work) dominates countervailing effects (e.g., job loss, employer noncompliance), guiding empirical design and interpretation.

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) study of the 1992 New Jersey minimum wage increase, comparing fast-food employment in New Jersey and Pennsylvania — This natural experiment provides direct causal evidence on employment effects of minimum wage increases in a low-wage urban labor market, challenging the traditional prediction of job losses.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis by Doucouliagos and Stanley (2009) on the employment effects of minimum wages, focusing on studies from 1972-2007 — A comprehensive meta-analysis synthesizes hundreds of estimates to determine the average effect size and publication bias, offering a robust assessment of the hypothesis across multiple contexts.

[PATH:theoretical] Monopsony labor market models (e.g., Manning, 2003) applied to urban low-wage markets — These models show that when employers have market power, a moderate minimum wage can increase employment rather than reduce it, providing a theoretical framework to refute the simple negative employment effect hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Azar, J., Marinescu, I., & Steinbaum, M. (2020). Labor market concentration. Journal of Human Resources, 55(4), 1211-1244. (and related working papers by the same authors using online job vacancy data) — This line of research directly measures employer concentration across U.S. local labor markets and estimates its effect on wage setting and hiring. Combining these concentration measures with state-level minimum wage changes and product market competition proxies (e.g., import penetration, industry concentration) would allow a direct test of whether the hiring reduction from a minimum wage increase is smaller in markets where firms face competitive pressure on prices.

[PATH:empirical] Berger, D., Herkenhoff, K., & Mongey, S. (2022). Minimum wages, market power, and the product market. NBER Working Paper 30551. — This paper explicitly models and tests how product market competition moderates the employment effects of minimum wages. It provides both theoretical predictions and empirical evidence using U.S. data, making it directly relevant to the hypothesis. Examining its findings on the interaction between product market power and minimum wage pass-through would either support or challenge the claim.
